extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and media studies researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the distinguishing features and dimensions that make a news story 'hard' or 'soft'—for use by journalists, teachers, students, and media researchers when classifying or producing news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: timeliness and consequentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news is journalistic style and genre that focuses on events or incidents considered to be timely and consequential to people locally, regionally, nationally, or internationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics usually treated as hard news include politics, international affairs, economics, and science. Use this criterion to judge whether a story's subject matter and timing make it socially or politically consequential rather than primarily entertaining or feature-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic/domain criterion (typical hard vs soft topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject areas are generally regarded as hard news (politics, international affairs, economics, science) while others are typically regarded as soft news (entertainment, arts, celebrities, culture-related subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that these are tendencies rather than absolute rules: some topics (e.g., natural disasters) are variably classified by different researchers. Historically, 'soft news' referred to feature articles but has broadened to include many human-interest and culture topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness/urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news tends to be time-sensitive and urgent, with coverage of reported events or specific topics quickly becoming outdated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recency and the story's susceptibility to rapid obsolescence as an indicator of hardness; breaking events and immediate developments score high on this metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting style: objectivity vs subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news is associated with objective reporting, whereas soft news is considered more individualized and subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story emphasizes detached, fact-centered presentation (hard) or personalization, opinion, and entertainment values (soft). Stylistic signals—tone, explicit subjectivity, and reliance on emotional framing—indicate softer reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinemann — topic dimension (political relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of a three-dimension model: the more politically relevant a news item is, the 'harder' it is judged to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political relevance directly—coverage tied to policy, governance, elections, or public affairs raises 'hardness' on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinemann — focus dimension (societal consequences vs episodic individual focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which coverage focuses on societal consequences (hard) versus individuals and episodic framing (soft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories framed around broader social impacts, structural explanations, or policy implications are harder; stories framed around individual anecdotes, personal experiences, or episodic accounts are softer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinemann — style dimension (impersonal/unemotional vs personal/emotional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic dimension ranging from impersonal, unemotional presentation (hard) to personal, emotional, individualized presentation (soft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge language, narrative voice, and emotional appeals. Impersonal, neutral diction and emphasis on facts indicate hardness; evocative, emotional language and personalization indicate softness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum and blending (degree of hardness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard and soft news are not wholly distinct categories but exist on a continuum; techniques are often blended in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify stories by degree rather than binary label. A traditionally hard topic (e.g., an election) can be 'softened' by focusing on personal experiences, and soft topics may include politically important information—use a proportional/hybrid assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest / feature orientation (soft-news characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft news tends to emphasize human-interest stories, features, celebrity/entertainment coverage, and culture-related subjects, historically linked to feature-article conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify prominence of human-centered storytelling, lifestyle angles, and entertainment framing when judging softness; historically, these were considered less important than hard news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment patterns and newsroom practice as an evaluative indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding: female journalists have historically been more likely than male journalists to be assigned soft-news topics; assignment patterns can reflect organizational biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distribution of assignments (who covers what beats) as a contextual metric for understanding how 'hard' or 'soft' a newsroom's coverage is and whether systemic biases shape topic allocation (e.g., statistics showing percent of crime or politics stories written by women).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and societal effects (political cynicism and mental well-being)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research-linked criterion: exposure to soft news has been associated with increased political cynicism and negative effects on democracy; hard news (generally more negative) and soft news consumption have also been linked to adverse effects on mental well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider downstream effects on audiences—if a story's framing or content is likely to increase cynicism or adversely affect well-being, that impact may factor into evaluations of the story's societal role and the responsibilities of journalists when choosing framing and prominence.
